I've got a dozen UHF radios but I've never found a good guide on how to learn them and nobody around here teaches it anymore.

It's all over the internet. Might even be growing in popularity (perhaps parallel to population). You'll need a decent antenna as high as you can get it and there are restrictions on that which vary based on where you live. Most hams have fun playing with different antenna designs, and you might be surprised what can work well.

In my area, I can easily listen to the repeater towers that city services use like police and fire. Might not be legally allowed to transmit, but you can legally listen. Some services use trunked systems which is a bit of a complex signal format, but a cheap USB SDR (Software Defined Radio) can do some clever tricks these days. Check out this site, and specifically OP25 - https://www.rtl-sdr.com/tutorial-on-setting-up-op25-for-p25-phase-2-digital-voice-decoding/

You might be able to get in touch with local radio clubs. They might take a membership fee or donation, then you can use their towers, not to mention the likelihood that they will share information with you, help you find really good deals on gear, show you more ways to engage, etc. Sometimes local community colleges have a radio club, but there may be some individually organized clubs which would benefit you more. Might even order a book on the first ham license level so you're allowed to tinker around and use more bands.

The first (and easiest) step into the radio world might be GMRS. It's a simple registration fee ($75?) with the FCC to get a call sign- no exams, good for 10 years, applies to the license holder's family (household) too. Basically, it lets you use higher power and more station types than someone with zero licensing who is restricted to low power walkie talkies. GMRS radios vary widely in price and a little in purpose (handheld, base, repeater, etc). Some GMRS repeater tower operators might give you permission to use their tower simply by asking.
